comparisons.peer_topic: Allowance for Credit Losses (ACL) Build and Offset
comparisons.peer_summary: Higher net credit losses were partially offset by a lower net build in the ACL, primarily due to a reduced build for transfer risk on non-U.S. exposures ($0.2 billion in 2024 vs. $1.9 billion in 2023), driven by U.S. banking law safety and soundness considerations.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and Bank of America discuss the components of their credit loss provisions/allowances, but focus on different drivers. Citigroup disclosed that higher net credit losses were partially offset by a lower net build in the allowance for credit losses (ACL), specifically noting a reduced build for transfer risk on non-U.S. exposures. Bank of America, in contrast, highlighted a decrease in its allowance driven by reserve releases in the commercial portfolio due to a favorable macroeconomic environment. While both reference allowance dynamics, BAC’s change was driven by portfolio-specific reserve releases and macro conditions, whereas Citi’s ACL build offset was driven by transfer risk adjustments for non-U.S. exposures.

The higher net credit losses were partially offset by a lower net build in the allowance for credit losses (ACL), primarily due to a smaller build related to transfer risk associated with exposures outside the U.S. (approximately $0.2 billion in 2024 versus $1.9 billion in 2023), driven by safety and soundness considerations under U.S. banking law.

GS highlights adverse charge-offs, while BAC highlights favorable reserve releases.
